utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good morning to everybody in and around the courtroom. Let's hope that the technology will not disappoint us. Mr. Registrar, will you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case IT-04-81-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Perisic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Could we have the appearances for the day, starting with the Prosecution, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, counsel, everyone in the courtroom. Mark Harmon, Barney Thomas, April Carter, and Carmela Javier for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. For the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone participating in the proceedings. Mr. Perisic today is represented by Mr. Gregor Guy-Smith and Mr. Novak Lukic. We have Deirdre Montgomery and Chad Mair, our assistants, with us today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Mr. Lukic. May the record show that the Chamber is sitting pursuant to Rule 15 bis today in Judge David's absence. Let me just welcome you back all. We haven't seen one another for a long time. I hope you are all okay and ready for about what you are to do. The Present hearing was really scheduled to solve all remaining outstanding issues before formally closing the trial or before, I guess, the Defence formally rests, more formal than the last time you did. And I will now move to the attempts on the agenda. I believe you all have a copy of the agenda. The first item that we really need to talk about are the MFI documents. On the 7th of February, 2011, the Trial Chamber, which was yesterday, issued an decision on the two pending Defence motions related to MFI documents, including the reconsideration motions, and the Trial Chamber was informed that there are still several documents in the trial record which still have an MFI status. The Chamber would like to know what the position of the parties is in this respect. Mr. Harmon, I think you have something to tell us on this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We will divide our submissions in respect of each of these agenda items. Ms. Carter will address that particular issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. In relation to the MFI documents, we have 48 outstanding Prosecution documents. We have been in continuous negotiations with the Defence to make sure we can cure some of the translation efforts. That has actually been completed as of yesterday. We will be filing a motion this afternoon. What that motion will entail will be 20 documents that we will seek to just remove the MFI. There will be 28 documents that we need to regulate the translations and upon that regulation we will seek to remove the MFI. There's also a third category --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let me understand. You said there's going to be a motion filed this afternoon. And of the 28 documents which you seek to regulate, are you still going to regulate after this motion or will they have been regulated by the time the motion is filed this afternoon?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: We have already uploaded all the appropriate documents into e-court, and we have listed the document IDs in our motion. And so once the Chamber orders the replacement of those document IDs, then we can actually have the MFI removed. So everything is ready and available upon the Court's discretion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Madam Carter. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: There's a third series of documents, of 24 documents, those are documents that have actually already been admitted into evidence; however, there has been a problem either due to a translation, missing pages, something is wrong actually with the document itself; we are seeking to regulate those documents as well. All 24 of those documents and their cures have been uploaded into e-court and are listed in detail in the motion that will be submitted today. And there's a final two documents --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just before we go to the two documents. Is it my understanding that the 24 documents were admitted into evidence notwithstanding those deficiencies?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Correct. They were already admitted into evidence. The -- what has been happening, as the Defence and the Prosecution have been drafting their final trial brief and going into detail in some of these documents, we're noticing some deficiency. And so both the Prosecution has identified some, the Defence has identified some, the Prosecution has subsequently submitted them all back to CLSS for revise, which has happened, and so we're asking just to change out those translations where needed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Okay. And then the final two documents are ones where they have been admitted; however, they contain extraneous pages that we'll just be seeking to remove from the trial record; they don't actually apply to the original document themselves. So in total we will have 74 documents that will be regulated through the Prosecution motion to be filed today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Madam Carter. What does this mean? We really can't then formally say we have rested until this motion is decided, these motions are decided?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, and when we get to other business, there's some other matters that need to be discussed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Really.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are you saying that these motions are not really holding us back -- they are not the only ones holding us back?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: There's one, but I'll discuss it when we get to the appropriate time. This matter should be resolved by today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Mr. Harmon. Mr. Lukic, do you have anything to say on what Madam Carter has been telling us?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. We have a full correspondence with the Prosecution, and towards the end of that process we will have all the results as reported to you by the Prosecution concerning the removal of the MFI designations. There is nothing further to say on our part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Lukic. Okay. Then the next item relates to the audio/video material related to transcripts for which the confidentiality has been lifted. Throughout the trial, the Trial Chamber has issued several decisions on the lifting of confidentiality of transcripts of testimony. The Registry informed the Trial Chamber that it is unclear whether the lifting of confidentiality should also be extended to audio/video material associated with those transcripts. Just before we answer the Registry, we would like to hear what the parties have to say on this point. I can guess what you are going to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, if the confidentiality has been lifted from the transcripts, it's from our point of view understandable that the confidentiality should also be lifted from the video material.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And you would confirm that, I see, Mr. Guy-Smith?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, we concur with that position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We'll advise the Registry accordingly. Thank you so much. The next item is Exhibit D666, a UN report on the Markale 1 incident, and it's in relation with the Sarajevo adjudicated facts from the Galic trial judgement. The Trial Chamber notes that in its decision of the 1st December 2010 it admitted into evidence, as Exhibit D666, the United Nations report related to the Markale 1 incident. In its bar table motion of the 5th of November, 2010, the Defence has indicated that the purpose for having this document admitted into evidence is to rebut the adjudicated facts related to that incident which were taken from the Galic case in the decision on the Prosecution's motion for judicial notice of adjudicated facts of Sarajevo dated the 26th of June, 2008. On the impact of the UN report on that adjudicated facts, the Trial Chamber deems it important to raise the following issues with the parties: The adjudicated facts concerning Sarajevo, in particular Fact 248, reflect the conclusion of the Galic Trial Chamber about the origin of fire in the Markale 1 incident. The Chamber notes that in the Galic judgement, such conclusion is preceded by an extensive discussion on the issue of the origin of the fire based on all the evidence of that case, which also includes the very UN report which is now in this case. Therefore, the Trial Chamber is of the view that the UN report cannot rebut the conclusion of the Galic judgement, as that conclusion was reached only after analysing the UN report and other evidence in that case. Therefore, to avoid any ambiguity in the trial record, the Trial Chamber is ready to -- well, first of all, the Trial Chamber would like to hear the parties on this issue as to how they propose the Trial Chamber should proceed. And I think on this point I would like to ask the Defence to start.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, it's the Defence position that this exhibit is an exhibit which is important for the Chamber's consideration. It's important for the consideration for two reasons: One is that it deals specifically with a report that has a factual finding which is, as you have pointed out, Your Honour, distinct from that which was found in the Galic judgement. However, be that as it may, this Chamber has the independent ability to make a determination of whether or not that particular fact has any import with regard to the decision that you are to make.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith, before -- we don't have control of the screen, and before this what you have said disappears, I would like to stop you and ask you a question. You say: "One is that it deals specifically with the report that has a factual finding which is, as you have pointed out, Your Honour, distinct from that which was found in the Galic judgement." Not quite sure I understand what you are saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, the report in D666 indicates in a number of different places that the origin of fire is impossible to determine. This is a statement that is made by a number of the different reporters within that particular report. And since the origin of fire obviously is an issue of some import with regard to that incident, we submit that the report -- when I'm saying distinct, is the report has information in it that is different from that which is contained in the Galic judgement. That's what I meant by distinct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yeah, okay. But that much we understand, Mr. Guy-Smith. But the point is, before adjudicating this fact, the Galic Trial Chamber was presented with a variety of evidence, amongst others this report. In considering the totality of that evidence as regards the origin of fire, the Galic Trial Chamber, by majority, came to the conclusion that it could make a determination about the origin of fire. What I'm saying is, it did consider this report amongst other evidence. Now, having the adjudicated fact from the Galic judgement and part of the evidence that the Galic Trial Chamber considered, challenging the adjudicated fact, it presents this Trial Chamber with a situation which has caused us to come back to you and say: What do you want us to do?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: What we want you to do in light of the totality of the evidence that exists with regard to this particular issue is to make an independent determination as to whether or not, after consideration of all the evidence at this point in time, those reports would impact your decision with regard to that issue. Understanding, understanding, of course, what you've said. I understand what you've said, but that's what we would like you to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: In addition, it also is germane to the issue of notice at the time whether or not, whether or not, our client could reasonably conclude based upon the information that was available at the time whether or not there was any conclusion with regard to the issue of the responsibles. So it has -- it has -- it also has --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You are flying far above me now.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, I certainly don't mean to be flying anywhere but with you, Your Honour. I know it's been a long time --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Please -- please take me along.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: It's been a long time since we've seen each other, but that's -- I want to be with you; we want to be on the same jet stream with you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: On this issue of notice, just ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just explain what do you mean by notice here; who is supposed to have got notice and at what?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: There's -- there's this underlying question that exists throughout the case as to what information -- what information may have been available to or was available to General Perisic and with that, how he would respond to that information obviously is one of the issues that the Chamber is going to have to be confronted with and have to deal with. So if you have conflicting reports with regard to a particular incident or if you have a report that says, for example, it was possible, and another one says it wasn't possible, impossible to make a determination, and if there's a connection between that particular information and our client, then obviously that would be something that would be germane for your consideration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I still don't understand notice.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, fine. Then let's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let's leave it like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Let me leave it alone. Let me leave it alone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yeah, leave it alone.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: The other thing is -- the other thing is - and I'm reminded by my colleagues - that what we have indicated is, this is a collection of documents produced by UN officers following the shelling incident known as Markale 1 on 5 February 1994, which is schedule incident A3, and the documents repeatedly conclude that based on the information available it's not possible to determine who was responsible for firing the shell.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Harmon, any response? Madam Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Defence rightfully points out that based on adjudicated facts it has the opportunity to lead rebuttal evidence, and we take no issue with that. However, in this particular instance, we would like to remind the Court of the statements of the Defence in relation to the scheduled incidents at the status hearing of September 2nd of 2008, and it's those statements that the Prosecution has seemingly detrimentally relied upon. When Mr. Lukic was discussing the adjudicated facts at page 281, beginning at line 10 and going through line 18, he indicated: "The Defence understands fully the need to expedite proceedings. We also understand the need to focus on what is essential to us in this trial, and that, as we heard awhile ago, is what the Prosecution is trying to prove. The Defence then, as now, has the following position: We do not want crime based evidence led before the Trial Chamber as long as any such crime based evidence can be seen to be a part of adjudicated facts. Our position is that in relation to all three kind of crimes, in cases where this is not led before the Trial Chamber, this has to be based on adjudicated facts." And it was with that understanding the Prosecution has led its case on many of the incidents, including Markale 3. And so while Defence is correct in law in relation to what can happen with relation to adjudicated facts, we would just like to remind the Chamber of their initial promises before this Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Madam Carter. Any reply? I guess, Mr. Lukic, you are going to be the one rising this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I was quoted now. I don't want to justify myself in any way, but that was 15 days after I was appointed as lead counsel in this trial, as you know, so it was in the process of the transition in the case. You know how we had to act during the trial, you know that certain issues were debated, and I think that this quotation of my words indicates, and it is a fact that what we indicated in the request, that this document be submitted as a bar table document, shows our intention which Mr. Guy-Smith mentioned in connection with certain facts which have been contested in this case and have to do with the awareness of Mr. Perisic of certain events which is an issue in this trial and which has been contested from the very beginning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What is this Trial Chamber supposed to do with your words, "I don't want to justify myself in any way, but that was 15 days after I was appointed as lead counsel in this trial, as you know, so it was in the process of the transition ..."? Surely you are not suggesting you're retracting what you promised in the beginning, what you say a minute after you've been appointed is what you say.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I want to say that you can understand that in that sense I do retract the statement which I gave at that point in time because it was a product of the fact that I had just been appointed lead counsel and I was faced at the moment with a series of issues that had to do with the further trial. We were faced with a series of issues that had to do with adjudicated facts and also with agreed facts. You are very well aware of this and you know that we had been conducting long negotiations about this with the Prosecutor's Office, and my intention was probably at the moment something that had to do with the course of the trial and what our expectations were. It was at the very beginning of the trial and probably it had to do with the pre-trial conferences at the very beginning and our wish to focus during the trial on what is essential. If at the moment I stated that adjudicated facts would not be a subject in this trial, we mostly stuck to that during most of the proceedings; but what is the issue that is being discussed right now and what we believe is important has do with something that is being contested in this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Excuse me. If I might, Your Honour, I'm going back to the Halcyon days of yesteryear, specifically the parts of the transcript that are being alluded to, and those words say exactly what they say but they are unfortunately taken out of context. The context in which this particular discussion was being had dealt with the fact that there had been a document filed in which the Defence and the Prosecution, without the permission or involvement of the accused, had reached an agreement. And it was within the context of agreed facts that this particular issue arose. And I'm looking at page 280 of the self-same transcript in which the matter is discussed. And as I'm sure the Chamber recalls, the issue of the agreed facts that concerned this particular matter was something that went on for quite some time and was an extremely sensitive issue that took considerable time to work out as between the Prosecution and the Defence. So I think that it would probably be fair to say that although the statement is being made, and I don't resolve from the words Mr. Lukic uttered nor do I think that he does, I think that they are being misinterpreted and being used in a global sense as opposed to being interpreted and analysed within the context in which that conversation had arose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now, I'm getting very worried. The more I hear what you guys are saying, the more I get worried. You are telling me now that you went and discussed and were -- and got into an agreement with the opposition without the involvement and permission of your client. That is a worrying position. But of course it is your responsibility. Number one. Number 2, I'm not quite sure -- because this is the context in which you say this took place, I'm not quite sure whether you are now saying you cannot be bound simply because you had not -- you did not have the permission of your client. And if that is what you are saying, my question would be: Did you tell your opposing number that in fact you don't have instructions that whatever agreement you are getting into is subject to approval by your client?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If I might, and I don't want to -- I don't want to take you down a road which we really don't need to go down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] -- we don't need to go down.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: We absolutely don't need to go down this road. But I think I can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You either had --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I think I can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You either had --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I think I can resolve the issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. If you go to page 280 of the transcript, it is very clear --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm technologically challenged, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm sorry, well, on September 2nd -- and I guess we'll have to go into private session because we were in private session --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just a second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. The Chamber will decide this matter. You still wanted to say something on this matter?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yeah, I just want to make sure that our point is clear, which is that, independent of what is said here, no promises were made by the Defence and there was never an assertion made by the Defence that we would not be challenging, in the normal process that one does, adjudicated facts. And I think that that interpretation of this statement is a bit stretched.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much, Mr. Guy-Smith. The next item was document ET 0469-3121 -- or 0469-3126, Exhibit 303, in the Martic trial judgement. This Exhibit 303 in the Martic judgement contains a list of victims for the Zagreb shelling and it is not in this -- in evidence in this case. And the Trial Chamber wanted to raise with the parties, just for the sake of completeness as to the number of victims that were -- may have been involved in the Zagreb shelling, whether the parties would have any comment about whether or not this document would be admitted into evidence. I'll start with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Your Honour, as a court exhibit, the Prosecution would have no objection. Obviously the Court is able to take into evidence whatever it seeks to, and the Prosecution has no objection to that. However, in transparency, we would like to note for the Court that the Prosecution actually sought to add this document to its exhibit list, to its 65 ter exhibit list, in a filing that was done on 30 June 2008 in front of the Pre-Trial Chamber. However, the Pre-Trial Chamber denied its addition to our 65 ter list. So we just want to make certain that the Court understands that the Prosecution did seek but was denied the same document in pre-trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Carter. Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Defence does not object to the admission. However, we want to state that according to the number checks we carried out, the numbers do not tally with those provided in the indictment concerning the Zagreb incident. That's the only thing we wanted to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. What is the difference, Mr. Lukic? What are the numbers?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Bear with me. We checked that yesterday. In relation to incident -- the incident of the 2nd of May, in this document it is stated that four people were killed and there were 146 people injured. In Schedule C, under 1, you see that the figures are different. As for the adjudicated facts in relation to Zagreb, we have the fact number 38 where the figures do not compare.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What does fact 38 say?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is from the Martic judgement, Adjudicated Fact 38: Five people were killed, they are stated by their first and last name, and that there were at least 160 injured. I believe the same situation concerns the incident of the 3rd of May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are you saying the incident of the 3rd of May also the figures don't tally?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. I guess obviously the Chamber will have to go back on that and look at it again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber will revisit this problem and see what the problems are, and we'll advise the parties accordingly. Item 7 relates to documents P2197 and 65 ter 7680, page 0622-0429. At page 14491 of the transcript, during the cross-examination of Mr. Ivan Djokic, the Prosecution quoted from Exhibit P2197, pages 0618-7722 and 0618-7723. While this entire exhibit has been admitted, the pages that the Prosecution cited have not been translated and uploaded into e-court. I don't know whether this was a deliberate intention on the part of the Prosecution. I see, Mr. Thomas, you are standing.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I can deal with this matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: The translation -- it has been translated. There is an English translation of that page. It wasn't uploaded in e-court at the time that Mr. Djokic was cross-examined. It is available and uploaded into e-court but it's not connected to the exhibit, and that, presumably, Your Honour, is because at the time P2197 was tendered, only certain portions were -- English portions were tendered with the complete B/C/S copy. This is a matter that we've discussed with our learned friends and there's agreement, as I understand it, between the parties that there's no problem with that English translation being available and uploaded into e-court and attached to the exhibit as it's presently tendered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I see Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, with regard to the exhibit as it stands, it's 2197, there are no difficulties with that occurring.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Then the Trial Chamber will ask the Registry to have the translation of these pages uploaded into e-court and attached to the exhibit. Thank you so much. Further, at page 14493 of the transcript, the Prosecution quoted from a document that has not been admitted, namely, 65 ter 7680, page 0622-0429. The document concerns another statement from Mr. Perisic regarding Mr. Djokic. What is the position of the parties?

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Well, sir, by way of explanation, this was a document which Mr. Djokic could not lay the appropriate foundation for. So at the time that Mr. Djokic was being cross-examined, the Prosecution was not in a position to be able to tender that document through him and so the document remains untendered. The Prosecution, therefore, didn't at that point feel that it had the ability to apply itself to tender that document as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Mr. Thomas. [Microphone not activated] -- I am sure -- sorry, I was speaking without my mike on. My apologies to the stenographer. I was saying I believe that brings the matter to a rest. I don't know whether you have anything to raise, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I would agree with Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Before we come to this last point, let me raise an issue which is not on the agenda and my apologies for it. It was brought to my attention this morning by Mr. Registrar. Mr. Registrar has brought to the attention of the Chamber the fact that in the decision on Ivan Djokic's expert report supporting materials admitted on, I think, the 3rd of February, 2011, a document, 65 ter number 07017D, which is Exhibit D805, document ID 140944, is part of the documents tendered. And Mr. Registrar notes that that document has a stipulation that all rights are reserved. And he says that once it goes into the database of the Tribunal it's available to all in sundry. And we wanted to just check with the parties whether the author's permission to publish had been obtained. This is a concern from the Registry. I can show you the hard copy for ease of -- and then you can also show the Prosecution, if they have not found it yet, in their -- in the electronic system. You'll see the highlighted portion of the document; it was highlighted by the Registry.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you for that. And the answer is, no, it was not. I will make inquiry and report back to the Chamber within -- safely within -- by Friday, as to whether or not we can obtain such permission or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And what shall we do with this in the meantime? We don't want it to go to all in sundry before you come back to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Right. Under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. It will be under seal in the meantime. Now, the Register advised that he saw this quite by chance. There hasn't been a concerted effort to check each and every document to see whether it does not fall under the same restrictions. Not only yours, everybody's. And the question is: Are we happy that our documents are okay in that respect?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I commend the Registrar for his eagle eyes, but I would hazard a guess that there are probably quite a few documents like this. And not only in our case but at the Tribunal. I'm not really sure how best to proceed, but I think we probably -- I think it would be fair to say we are happy. I think we should be relatively content that the situation that we've been, in the manner in which we've tendered documents and accepted documents, is appropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Harmon?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'm in the same position. I haven't gone back and reviewed all my documents, but I'm content to proceed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you so much. Finally -- not finally. Penultimate. The Trial Chamber would like to hear the parties before scheduling the submission of the final brief and the hearings of the closing argument what the parties want to suggest. We would like to have those final briefs, like, yesterday. Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, the parties have met and discussed these issues. We have reached agreement on all of these issues with one exception. I was advised by Mr. Lukic that there's a slight deviation from the first. We had agreed to propose to the the Court that closing briefs be due at the end of February. I know Mr. Lukic approached me before court and said he would like to change that proposal from the Defence's point of view to the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: -- 15th of February.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Slightly the other direction, Your Honour. To the 4th of March. So there's a difference in view between the two parties. In respect of the closing oral submissions, the parties agreed to propose to the Court that those be at the end of March. And there was a discussion in respect of the word limitation and the parties suggested to -- would like to suggest to the Court that there be a 100.000 word limit to each of the briefs. Those were the agreements and the discussions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And 100.000 would be what? Something like ... a lot of pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: It would be a lot of pages, Your Honour. There's no question about that. But this is a document-rich case. And I think because there are so many documents we were of the view that it merited an expansion. So those are the proposals that we have for the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And, Mr. Lukic, you confirm that you have moved now from end of February to 4th of March?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Just a few words, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because I wanted to put our arguments to you. When we discussed the limit of 100.000 words, both sides were faced with the fact that we have been working on these briefs for quite some time and it is for this reason that we are aware of the amount of documents and topics we both need to cover. As Mr. Harmon said, this is first and foremost a paper document trial, and many of them have barely been mentioned during the proceedings. This is our only opportunity to comment on such a great amount of documents which are in evidence. This is our first and most important document -- argument, for asking for 100.000 words. What we agreed on, as our joint wish, was to submit them by the 28th of February, which is a Monday, and we are now asking for a mere four days extra, that is to say, the 4th of March, because in the technical sense of editing the entire document, those four days would mean a lot to us. Another to bear in mind is that we are drafting a document in parallel in two languages because we keep informing Mr. Perisic constantly, which requires considerable effort and resources of the Defence. The same applies to our closing arguments. It is our wish, and I believe we are in agreement with the Prosecution, that after the briefs had been submitted, four weeks should be granted for the close of -- closing arguments, and we also need that time to translate for Mr. Perisic their entire brief, which will be as sizeable as ours, and we need that time to prepare ourselves for the final arguments -- closing arguments. I believe both sides also agree that one day each is sufficient for both parties to present their closing arguments. Those are our requests. And should you need any further information, we are at your disposal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon had convinced me on your behalf actually already, so I was going to grant all those requests. But thank you for the arguments. Thank you so much. 4th of March then it will be. And 28th to 31st of March it will be, closing arguments. Okay. It is then so ordered that the parties will file their closing briefs by no later than the 4th of March, 2011, and that closing arguments will be scheduled for hearing on the 28th to the 31st of March. Parties are granted 100.000 word limit each and are granted a day each to present their argument. Thank you so much. Is there any other item that any of the parties would like to raise which was not on the agenda? Or which was on the agenda but you are not satisfied with.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have two items to raise. The first is -- in agreement with the Defence as well, Ms. Carter mentioned it initially, as we go through these documents and prepare these briefs, we note occasionally that there are translations that are incorrect, inaccurate. And we want to reserve the right to upload corrected versions. We think it's important that the Chamber have the corrected translations; we think it's important that the parties have corrected translations and that we operate off as accurate a record as we can. So the first item is: We would request the opportunity to substitute documents with accurate translations should we find some documents that need to be modified and retranslated. That's the first request we have. And we propose to proceed in the manner in which we have worked previously, that is, if the Defence finds a document or if the Prosecution finds a document, that we'd identify an error in the translation, we would discuss it with the other side, we'd reach an agreement, and then we would request the Trial Chamber's permission to upload that accurate translation into the trial record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And this accurate translation is by an agreement between the parties without the involvement of CLSS?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, we would submit them to CLSS for revisions, and then once we got that we would discuss it amongst the parties. And once we reach the agreement, we would seek to upload the accurate translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I agree fully and I support what Mr. Harmon just said. And there's something that we already established in practice, and I wanted to ask for a change in the files already: Exhibit P191 is the Law on the Army of the Republic of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Have you moved away from correcting translations? Are you now on a different issue? Okay. The Law on the Army exhibit, P191 ...

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] P191, the Law on the Army of Republika Srpska. While working on the brief, we noticed that Article 4 of the law is problematic and that the English translation does not match the Serbian original. We asked for official translation from CLSS, we discussed this with our colleagues from the Prosecution --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Slow down. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They agree that Article 4 as it is should be substituted by a new translation. We have uploaded it into e-court with 1D21-0221; that is the new number. And we would just ask for the existing new translation to be substituted only in terms of Article 4. So Article 4 should be substituted from the previous translation with the new one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Any comment, Madam Carter?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I agreed with the Defence this morning on that specific exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much . Mr. Harmon, you had mentioned the first of two items you wanted to raise.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I have two items. I should be more robust in my description. Mr. Thomas has one item and Ms. Carter has one item. But let me -- I need to go into private session to discuss my second item.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Madam Carter, I guess this is going to be your turn.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. On 7 February 2011, the Chamber issued its decision on Mr. Perisic's second and third motions regarding MFI documents. At that time it reserved its ruling in relation to D510 because the Prosecution had noted that it anticipated a stipulation. I believe the stipulation has now been agreed upon, and I'd like to read it into the record. The stipulation in regards to D510 is that the parties stipulate that the initials noted after the first handwritten note in the top-right corner of Exhibit D510 are "MP" which corresponds to Momcilo Perisic. With the agreement of the Defence, if that stipulation has been reached, the Prosecution no longer has any objection to D510 and would be happy for the MFI document -- or MFI designation to be removed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, we have agreed to this stipulation, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Registrar, may the MFI status of the document please be removed and be given an exhibit number. I guess the exhibit number would be D510.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document becomes Exhibit D510. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Mr. Registrar. Is that all? Any outstanding --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Any outstanding -- thank you very much, Mr. Harmon. -- outstanding items on your side, Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Two more items, Your Honour. In P1196 there's something that should be added. We need to add the English translation to it, which is why in transcript T-13073/5 it was decided to wait until translation is submitted, so we propose that the doc ID be 1D21-0220. During the testimony of Witness Novakovic, it was requested that an official translation be submitted. It is Article 36 of the Law on Defence of the Republic of Serbian Krajina. Article 34. Article 34 is what I said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now -- sorry about that. Do we have the translation now? Thank you so much. And now all you want is the translation to be added? That's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that is all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. I guess there's no objection from the opposite side?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: There is no objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. The translation may be added.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And another issue that the Defence would propose. We have discussed it with our colleagues from the Prosecution. The Law on the Serbian Army of Krajina, as opposed to the Law on Army of Republika Srpska and the Law on the Army of Yugoslavia, which have been admitted in entirety both in B/C/S and in English, this Law on the Serbian Army of Krajina has only been admitted in terms of several paragraphs during the testimony of a witness. And while working on the final brief, we propose that as D170 includes the entire law in B/C/S, it's already uploaded, that what could be added to the English translation would be certain articles from the law. Not the whole law, because the law has around 300 articles and is not essential for this trial, but roughly around 60 or 70 articles which we believe are relevant in various ways for this trial is what we have received in translation officially through CLSS. We have of informed the Trial Chamber about this, and we would like to add this translation to the existing Exhibit D170 because we wish, during our final brief and final arguments, use certain elements from this law. We believe that it's very relevant because as you can see the other two laws have been admitted in their entirety because of relevance. Therefore, we have uploaded this in e-court, and it's ready to be included as one of the exhibits. I mean all of the English translation that we have now. Let me just also note, without confusing matters, Exhibit D1 -- D85 and D90 are specific articles of this same law. We believe - and I think we have discussed this with the Registrar - that the entire Law of the Serbian Army of Krajina, just like the Law on Army of Republika Srpska and the Law on the Army of Yugoslavia, should be given one single number and we suggested it should be D170. And then it would include both the B/C/S and English translation of all the articles which would then be matching and all included in one document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Any comment from the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time the Prosecution is in agreement with the Defence that that is the appropriate course of action; however, it's been unable to have the opportunity to actually look at the three exhibits to ensure that the final exhibit, D170, does in fact contain all of the specific articles.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Articles D85, D90.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Exactly. So in principal we are in agreement. However, we would like the opportunity to have a look after court to make sure that we do have a complete document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Have you seen the English translation of the articles that the Defence proposed to upload?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: It was sent to me last night.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And you are happy with that, that they haven't left anything that you would have wanted to translate?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: No, it's simply a matter of that there are a number of different documents that are outstanding and then they wanted to merge all into one single document, and I just want to make sure, again, that we have actually picked up all the appropriate laws.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can I suggest that when you have picked up all the appropriate laws you give a note to the Registrar so that the Registrar can do the necessary.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Absolutely, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar is asking what then do we do with D85 and D90. I would imagine that once we have a consolidated exhibit we can withdraw those two.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that would be the best thing to do. On the other hand, however, once you go back to the transcript, where, for example, reference is made to those exhibits, what conclusions you would eventually draw? I don't think it would be any hindrance to leave the previous two in addition to the consolidated one. Perhaps just retain the exhibit numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Mr. Registrar will deal with that. Is that all, Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I believe so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And that's all also from the Prosecution side. Okay. Thank you very much. And at this stage that brings us to the conclusion of our session today. And Chamber stands adjourned sine die.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 11.35 a.m.
